newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street turns cautious after Greenspan warning.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street turns cautious after Greenspan warning.

text.p: The caution level on Wall Street has gone up a notch or two after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning that it was time to be wary about "irrational exuberance" in the markets.

Although Greenspan did not refer specifically to stocks, traders said the Fed chairman was clearly talking about the U.S. stock market, where key market barometers have advanced about 25 percent this year.
"It was his way of firing a shot across the bow of the financial markets to try to reduce the level of speculation," said Hugh Johnson, market strategist at First Albany Co.

Johnson said there is some speculation driving stocks but it is not yet at the "later, more dangerous stages." He theorized that Greenspan was concerned that speculation may intensify and affect the real economy, first by feeding inflation and then by accelerating a downturn when the bubble bursts.

Johnson said he is a little more cautious following Greenspan's Thursday night speech but he has not made a major shift in his views. The analyst expects U.S. stocks to spend time consolidating their gains and then rise at a much more moderate pace in 1997.
While Johnson became somewhat more cautious, market analyst Robert Stovall changed his short-term outlook Friday to negative from neutral.
Stovall, head of Stovall/Twenty-First Advisers, said the change is "based on valuations rising to a point where the market is vulnerable to any disappointments or upsets."

He said that for seasonal reasons if there is a disappointment in coming weeks, any downturn could be exacerbated. He reasoned that investors have become accustomed to the stock market rising in December and January, so any sell-off in the next few weeks would be that much more painful.

As for Greenspan's now-famous comment about the danger of "irrational exuberance," Stovall noted that it was not the first time a Fed chairman turned his guns on stock market speculation. He recalled that in the 1960s then-Chairman William McChesney Martin had a "brief but noticeable impact" when he warned about speculation in a group of stocks running up on enthusiasm about the "space race" with the Soviet Union.
In the longer term, Stovall said, underlying factors remain positive for stocks.

Stanely Nabi, vice chairman at Wood Struthers & Winthrop, said Greenspan has voiced concerns about excesses in the stock market before. But after a sharp run-up in November, he said, the market was more willing to listen.
Barring an outside surprise, Nabi thinks it will be "off to the races again" but at a more subdued pace.

Bonds and the dollar joined stocks in their broad retreat early Friday, but all three markets saw recoveries as the day wore on. The Dow industrials recovered about two-thirds of their losses to end down 55 Friday at 6,382.

John McCarthy, senior vice president for foreign exchange at ING Baring Capital Markets in New York, said a rise in the dollar has indeed accompanied the U.S. stock market over the last two years but the currency markets are focusing on other issues.

He said the dollar could get a lift Monday from a strong hint from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Sunday that he will stay on board in President Clinton's cabinet. "That's positive for the dollar in the short term; he's done a very credible job," McCarthy said.

McCarthy said the vast holdings of dollar reserves by Asian central banks is probably more of a negative for the dollar than speculation in the stock market. But he said Greenspan was clearly bent on avoiding a repetition of what happened in Japan when the Nikkei-225 index soared to nearly 40,000 in 1989, only to lose half its value in 1990.
John Breazeale, a money manager based in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., said it has been "an accepted proposition that the equity markets are operating on speculation."
Breazeale, president of Weiss Money Management Inc., said he has been teling even fixed-income investors to move to the sidelines by going to Treasury bills.

"We think the potential for a large problem is out there that could affect both the bond market and the equity market," he said. He is concerned that foreign buyers may reduce their purchases of Treasury bonds. Thus, he said, long-term interest rates could rise even without an inflation problem.

Johnson and other analysts pointed out that one reason for the retreat from Friday's early losses was news that the jobless rate rose to 5.4 percent in November from 5.2 percent, while creation of new jobs was well below forecasts. The analysts said the data made an interest rate hike in mid-December unlikely.
